title: Malta Year 8 Math — All 19 Chapters: Basic Set B
question: Set B: one quick step from each of the nineteen chapters, with new numbers.
intro: **Set B:** the same 38 steps as Basic, new questions, two per chapter.

questions.title: Ch 1 Directed Numbers · Kinnie on the table
questions.prompt:
A bottle of Kinnie comes out of the freezer at \(-5\,^\circ\text{C}\) (5 degrees below zero).

On the table it gets 7 degrees warmer.

What is its temperature now?
questions.figure_alt: A thermometer from −6 to 6 °C next to a Kinnie bottle. The start −5 is marked; an arrow goes 7 degrees up to a question mark.
questions.solution:
Warmer means move **up** the thermometer:

\[-5 + 7 = \boxed{2}\]

\(-12\) moves 7 degrees colder instead of warmer; \(12\) forgets the minus sign on \(-5\).

questions.title: Ch 1 Directed Numbers · Hotel lift down
questions.prompt:
In a hotel in St Julian's, floor 0 is the street and floor \(-1\) is 1 floor below it.

A lift starts on floor \(-1\) and goes down 3 floors.

Which floor does it stop at?
questions.figure_alt: A building with floors −5 to 3 and street level at floor 0. A lift car is on floor −1 and an arrow goes down 3 floors to a floor marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Down means subtract:

\[-1 - 3 = \boxed{-4}\]

\(2\) moves 3 floors up instead of down.

questions.title: Ch 2 Number Work · Kinnie crates
questions.prompt:
You have 4 bottles of Kinnie and 2 crates with 6 bottles in each crate.

The total is \(4 + 2\times6\).

How many bottles are there?
questions.figure_alt: Four loose bottles plus two crates with six bottles each, then equals a question mark.
questions.solution:
BIDMAS: multiply first (the crates), then add.

\[2\times6 = 12\]

\[4 + 12 = \boxed{16}\]

\(36\) adds first, as if it were \((4 + 2)\times6\).

questions.title: Ch 2 Number Work · Square cake
questions.prompt:
A square birthday cake is cut into 5 rows with 5 pieces in each row.

The number of pieces is \(5^2\) (the small 2 means 5 times itself).

How many pieces are there?
questions.figure_alt: A 5 by 5 square of pieces; how many pieces in all is the question.
questions.solution:
A square number is rows times columns:

\[5^2 = 5\times5\]

\[5\times5 = \boxed{25}\]

\(10\) is \(5\times2\), not \(5\times5\).

questions.title: Ch 3 Angles · Ladder on a wall
questions.prompt:
A ladder leans on a wall and stands on flat ground.

On the wall side, the ladder makes \(65^\circ\) with the ground.

Find the angle between the ladder and the ground on the other side.
questions.figure_alt: A ladder leaning on a wall. Between the ladder and the ground on the wall side is 65°; on the other side the angle is a question mark.
questions.solution:
The ground is a straight line, so the two angles add up to \(180^\circ\):

\[180^\circ - 65^\circ = \boxed{115^\circ}\]

\(25^\circ\) uses \(90^\circ\), which is for a right angle, not a straight line.

questions.title: Ch 3 Angles · House roof
questions.prompt:
The roof of a house is a triangle.

The two bottom angles are \(35^\circ\) each.

Find the top angle.
questions.figure_alt: A house with a triangular roof. Both bottom corners of the roof are 35°; the top angle is a question mark.
questions.solution:
The angles in a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\):

\[180^\circ - 35^\circ - 35^\circ = \boxed{110^\circ}\]

\(145^\circ\) takes away only one of the two \(35^\circ\) angles.

questions.title: Ch 4 Fractions · Chocolate bar
questions.prompt:
A chocolate bar has 12 equal pieces.

A fraction like \(\frac{1}{12}\) means 1 piece out of the 12.

You eat 4 pieces and a friend eats 3 pieces.

What fraction of the bar is eaten?
questions.figure_alt: A chocolate bar of 12 pieces: 4 orange pieces (you), 3 green pieces (a friend); the eaten fraction is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Same size pieces, so add the tops:

\[\frac{4}{12} + \frac{3}{12} = \boxed{\frac{7}{12}}\]

\(\frac{7}{24}\) adds the bottoms too, but there are still 12 pieces, not 24.

questions.title: Ch 4 Fractions · Bus seats
questions.prompt:
A Valletta bus has 24 seats.

\(\frac{3}{4}\) of the seats are taken (\(\frac{3}{4}\) means 3 out of every 4 equal parts).

How many seats are taken?
questions.figure_alt: 24 seats in 4 equal boxes of 6; 3 boxes are shaded and labelled with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Split 24 into 4 equal boxes, then take 3 of them:

\[24\div4 = 6\]

\[6\times3 = \boxed{18}\]

\(6\) is only one box; you need 3 of the 4 boxes.

questions.title: Ch 5 Decimals · Ice cream and water
questions.prompt:
An ice cream costs €2.20 and a bottle of water costs €1.75.

How much do they cost together?
questions.figure_alt: A ice cream with a price tag of €2.20 and a water with a price tag of €1.75; beside them the column sum 2.20 + 1.75 with a question mark for the total.
questions.solution:
Line up the decimal points:

\[2.20 + 1.75 = \boxed{3.95}\]

- The answer is €3.95.
- \(1.97\) writes 2.20 as 0.22 (\(0.22 + 1.75\)) instead of lining up the decimal points.

questions.title: Ch 5 Decimals · Cans of drink
questions.prompt:
One can holds 0.33 litres of drink.

A pack has 10 cans, so it holds \(0.33\times10\) litres.

How many litres are in the pack?
questions.figure_alt: Ten items of 0.33 litres each in a row; below, a place-value table with 0.33 in the top row and arrows moving each digit one place left into a row of question marks.
questions.solution:
Every digit moves one place to the left:

\[0.33\times10 = \boxed{3.3}\]

\(0.033\) moves the digits to the right, which is dividing by 10.

questions.title: Ch 6 Percentages · Walk to school
questions.prompt:
A class has 30 students.

\(10\%\) of them walk to school (\(10\%\) means 10 out of every 100, the same as one tenth).

How many students walk to school?
questions.figure_alt: A bar for 30 students cut into 10 equal blocks; the first block (10%) is a question mark.
questions.solution:
\(10\%\) is one block out of 10:

\[30\div10 = \boxed{3}\]

- So \(10\%\) of 30 students is 3 students.
- \(20\) takes 10 away; a percentage is a part, not a subtraction.

questions.title: Ch 6 Percentages · Blue floor tiles
questions.prompt:
A floor has 100 equal tiles in a 10 by 10 square.

Some tiles are blue.

Per cent means out of 100.

What percentage of the floor is blue?
questions.figure_alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 tiles: 2 full columns and 3 more are coloured.
questions.solution:
- Per cent means out of 100.
- Count: 2 full columns and 3 more.

\[20 + 3 = 23\]

\[\frac{23}{100} = \boxed{23\%}\]

\(77\%\) counts the white tiles.

questions.title: Ch 7 Ratio · Pocket money
questions.prompt:
You and your brother share €30 in the ratio \(2 : 3\).

Your brother gets the bigger share.

How many euros does he get?
questions.figure_alt: A bar model: two green boxes for you, three yellow boxes for your brother, €30 in all; the brother's share is a question mark.
questions.solution:
There are \(2 + 3 = 5\) equal parts:

\[30\div5 = 6\]

\[6\times3 = \boxed{18}\]

So the bigger share is €18.

€12 is the smaller share; €15 splits €30 into 2 halves, but the ratio has 5 parts, not 2.

questions.title: Ch 7 Ratio · Ferry cars and vans
questions.prompt:
On the Gozo ferry there are 30 cars and 12 vans.

Write the ratio cars : vans, \(30 : 12\), in its simplest form.
questions.figure_alt: Thirty blue counters (cars) in 5 groups of 6 and twelve green counters (vans) in 2 groups of 6.
questions.solution:
The HCF of 30 and 12 is 6:

\[30\div6 = 5\]

\[12\div6 = 2\]

\[\boxed{5 : 2}\]

- \(15 : 6\) and \(10 : 4\) are the same ratio, but they can still be divided by 3 or by 2.
- \(2 : 5\) swaps the order: cars come first.

questions.title: Ch 8 Algebra · Bus stop
questions.prompt:
There are \(x\) passengers on a bus.

At the next stop 6 more get on, and now there are 17 passengers, so \(x + 6 = 17\).

Solve to find \(x\).
questions.figure_alt: A bus with x passengers; six people get on, and then there are 17 passengers; x is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Take 6 from both sides:

\[x + 6 = 17\]

\[x = 17 - 6\]

\[x = \boxed{11}\]

23 adds 6 instead of taking it away.

questions.title: Ch 8 Algebra · Chairs at tables
questions.prompt:
Long tables are pushed together in a row for a festa dinner, with 2 chairs on each long side of a table and 1 chair at each end of the row.

For \(t\) tables you need \(4t + 2\) chairs, where \(4t + 2\) means \(4\times t + 2\).

How many chairs do 5 tables need?
questions.figure_alt: A function machine: 5 tables go in, times 4, plus 2, and the number of chairs is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Put 5 in place of \(t\), multiply first, then add:

\[4\times5 = 20\]

\[20 + 2 = \boxed{22}\]

47 reads \(4t\) as 45, but \(4t\) means \(4\times t\).

questions.title: Ch 9 Sequences · Tables and chairs
questions.prompt:
Square tables are pushed together in a row, with chairs all round.

1 table has 4 chairs, 2 tables have 6 chairs and 3 tables have 8 chairs.

How many chairs fit round 4 tables?
questions.figure_alt: Square tables in a row with chairs round them: 1, 2 and 3 tables with 4, 6 and 8 chairs; pattern 4 is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Each new pattern adds 2 chairs:

\[8 + 2 = \boxed{10}\]

12 adds 4 chairs for the new table, but the chair at the join moves to the end, so only 2 are new.

questions.title: Ch 9 Sequences · Festa arches
questions.prompt:
Each festa arch has light bulbs.

Arch number \(n\) has \(4n + 1\) bulbs, where \(4n + 1\) means \(4\times n + 1\).

How many bulbs are on arch 5?
questions.figure_alt: A table: arches 1, 2, 3 have 5, 9, 13 bulbs (each +4); arch 5 is a question mark. The rule is 4n + 1.
questions.solution:
Put \(n = 5\) into the rule, multiply first, then add:

\[4\times5 = 20\]

\[20 + 1 = \boxed{21}\]

10 reads \(4n\) as 4 + 5, but \(4n\) means \(4\times n\).

questions.title: Ch 10 Circles · Dinner plate
questions.prompt:
A round dinner plate has radius 13 cm.

Find its diameter.
questions.figure_alt: A round plate with a 13 cm radius from the centre and a dashed diameter across it.
questions.solution:
The diameter goes right across, so it is two radii:

\[d = 2r\]

\[d = 2\times13\]

\[d = \boxed{26 \text{ cm}}\]

6.5 cm halves the radius; the diameter is double, not half.

questions.title: Ch 10 Circles · Cake tin
questions.prompt:
A round cake tin has diameter 20 cm.

You tie a ribbon once round it.

Use \(\pi \approx 3.14\) to find the length of ribbon (the circumference).
questions.figure_alt: A round cake of diameter 20 cm rolled out into a straight line a little more than 3 diameters long.
questions.solution:
The circumference is about 3.14 diameters:

\[C = \pi d\]

\[C \approx 3.14\times20\]

\[C \approx \boxed{62.8 \text{ cm}}\]

31.4 cm uses the radius (10 cm) instead of the diameter, so it is only half way round.

questions.title: Ch 11 Perimeter & Area · Classroom floor
questions.prompt:
A classroom floor is 7 m long and 6 m wide.

Find its area.
questions.figure_alt: A 7 m by 6 m floor split into 1 m squares.
questions.solution:
Rows of squares:

\[A = l\times w\]

\[A = 7\times6\]

\[A = \boxed{42 \text{ m}^2}\]

26 m is the perimeter (the distance round), not the area.

questions.title: Ch 11 Perimeter & Area · Boat sail
questions.prompt:
A boat sail is a right-angled triangle.

Its base is 6 m and its height up the mast is 9 m.

Find its area.
questions.figure_alt: A right-angled triangle with base 6 m and height 9 m up the left side, inside a dashed 6 by 9 rectangle on a grid.
questions.solution:
A triangle is half of its rectangle:

\[A = \tfrac{1}{2}bh\]

\[A = \tfrac{1}{2}\times6\times9\]

\[A = \boxed{27 \text{ m}^2}\]

54 m² forgets the half.

questions.title: Ch 12 Surface Area & Nets · Ice cube
questions.prompt:
A large ice cube has edges of 4 cm.

Find its surface area.
questions.figure_alt: A cube with 4 cm edges and a net of six squares in a staircase shape.
questions.solution:
6 square faces, each:

\[\begin{aligned} 4\times4 &= 16 \text{ cm}^2 \\ SA &= 6a^2 \end{aligned}\]

\[SA = 6\times16\]

\[SA = \boxed{96 \text{ cm}^2}\]

64 cm³ is the volume 4 × 4 × 4; surface area covers the outside.

questions.title: Ch 12 Surface Area & Nets · Water tank
questions.prompt:
A water tank on a roof is 3 m long, 2 m wide and 2 m high.

Find its volume.
questions.figure_alt: A cuboid 3 by 2 by 2 built from 1 m cubes.
questions.solution:
Count the cubes, layer by layer:

\[V = lwh\]

\[V = 3\times2\times2\]

\[V = \boxed{12 \text{ m}^3}\]

7 m³ adds the three lengths; volume multiplies them.

questions.title: Ch 13 Graphs · Cinema seat
questions.prompt:
A cinema seating plan is drawn on a grid.

Your seat is at point S.

What are the coordinates of S?
questions.figure_alt: A coordinate grid from 0 to 6 across and 0 to 5 up with point S plotted next to a small picture.
questions.solution:
From 0 go 2 across, then 4 up:

\[\boxed{(2, 4)}\]

\((4, 2)\) reads up before across.

questions.title: Ch 13 Graphs · Taxi fare
questions.prompt:
A taxi costs €2 to start plus €3 for each kilometre.

The cost is \(y = 3x + 2\) euros for \(x\) km.

Find \(y\) when \(x = 2\).
questions.figure_alt: The line y = 3x + 2 on a grid; a dashed line from x = 2 goes up to the line at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Put \(x = 2\) into the rule:

\[y = 3\times2 + 2\]

\[y = 6 + 2\]

\[y = \boxed{8}\]

- The answer is €8.
- \(10\) adds \(3 + 2\) first and then multiplies by 2: multiply first.

questions.title: Ch 14 Statistics · Shoe sizes
questions.prompt:
A group of friends wear these shoe sizes: \(37, 38, 38, 36, 38, 39, 37\).

Find the mode.
questions.figure_alt: A dot plot of 37, 38, 38, 36, 38, 39, 37: the column above 38 is the tallest.
questions.solution:
The mode is the value that appears most often: 38 appears 3 times.

\[\text{mode} = \boxed{38}\]

\(3\) is how many times 38 appears, not the value itself.

questions.title: Ch 14 Statistics · Cycling
questions.prompt:
You cycle 5 km, 9 km and 7 km on three days.

Find the mean distance per day.
questions.figure_alt: A bar chart of 5, 9, 7; the mean, the level height, is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Add them, then share equally between the 3 values:

\[5 + 9 + 7 = 21\]

\[21\div3 = \boxed{7}\]

\(21\) is the total; the mean shares it out.

questions.title: Ch 15 Probability · Jar of marbles
questions.prompt:
A jar holds 5 green and 4 yellow marbles.

One marble is taken without looking.

What is the probability that it is green?
questions.figure_alt: Jar of marbles: 5 green and 4 yellow; the probability is a question mark.
questions.solution:
5 green out of:

\[\begin{aligned} 5 + 4 &= 9 \\ P(\text{green}) &= \boxed{\frac{5}{9}} \end{aligned}\]

\(\frac{5}{4}\) compares green with yellow; a probability compares with **all** 9 marbles.

questions.title: Ch 15 Probability · Coloured cards
questions.prompt:
Ten cards are shuffled face down: 3 are green and 7 are red.

You turn over one card.

What is the probability that it is **not** green?
questions.figure_alt: Ten cards: 3 green and 7 red.
questions.solution:
\[P(\text{not green}) = 1 - \frac{3}{10}\]

\[P(\text{not green}) = \boxed{\frac{7}{10}}\]

- \(\frac{3}{10}\) is P(green) itself.
- \(\frac{10}{7}\) is more than 1, and no probability is more than 1.

questions.title: Ch 16 Constructions · Wooden sticks
questions.prompt:
You glue three wooden sticks into a triangle.

Which three lengths can make a triangle?
questions.figure_alt: A base of 5 cm with compass arcs of 2 cm and 2 cm from its ends; the arcs leave a gap and never meet.
questions.solution_title: The two short sides must reach
questions.solution:
The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest:

\[5 + 6 = 11\]

\[11 > 9\]

- So \(\boxed{5 \text{ cm}, 6 \text{ cm}, 9 \text{ cm}}\) works.
- In the others the short sides are too short: \(2 + 2 = 4\), \(3 + 5 = 8\) and \(1 + 6 = 7\), each less than the longest side.

questions.title: Ch 16 Constructions · Folded page
questions.prompt:
The corner of a page is a right angle, \(90^\circ\).

You fold the corner so the fold line bisects the angle.

What is each smaller angle?
questions.figure_alt: An angle of 90° with a dashed bisector splitting it into two equal angles marked with question marks.
questions.solution:
Bisect means cut into two equal halves:

\[90^\circ\div2 = \boxed{45^\circ}\]

\(180^\circ\) doubles instead of halving.

questions.title: Ch 17 Transformations · Lake reflection
questions.prompt:
The calm surface of a lake is the \(x\)-axis.

The top of a tree is at \((4, 3)\).

Where is the top of its reflection in the water?
questions.figure_alt: A grid with the x-axis as a mirror; the point (4, 3) and a dashed arrow to a question mark on the other side.
questions.solution:
The \(x\)-axis is the mirror: \(y\) changes sign, \(x\) stays.

\[(4, 3) \to \boxed{(4, -3)}\]

\((-4, 3)\) reflects in the \(y\)-axis instead.

questions.title: Ch 17 Transformations · Warehouse robot
questions.prompt:
A robot in a warehouse is at \((5, 3)\).

It moves by \(\binom{-2}{1}\): 2 left and 1 up.

Where does it stop?
questions.figure_alt: A grid with the point (5, 3), a move of 2 left and 1 up ending at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Add the moves to the coordinates:

\[(5 - 2,\ 3 + 1) = \boxed{(3, 4)}\]

\((-2, 1)\) is the move itself, not where the point lands.

questions.title: Ch 18 Real-life Problems · Beach kiosk
questions.prompt:
At a beach kiosk the bill is €4.55.

You pay with a €10 note.

How much change do you get?
questions.figure_alt: A receipt with a total of €4.55 next to a €10 note; the change is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Change = money paid − cost:

\[10.00 - 4.55 = \boxed{5.45}\]

- The change is €5.45.
- \(6.55\) takes away only the 4 euros and copies the cents instead of taking them away too.

questions.title: Ch 18 Real-life Problems · Lunch break
questions.prompt:
The school lunch break starts at 12:50 and lessons start again at 13:20.

How many minutes is the break?
questions.figure_alt: Two clocks: 12:50 and 13:20, with an arrow between them marked question mark minutes.
questions.solution:
Count up to the hour, then on:

\[12{:}50 \to 13{:}00 = 10 \text{ min}\]

\[13{:}00 \to 13{:}20 = 20 \text{ min}\]

\[10 + 20 = \boxed{30 \text{ min}}\]

\(70\) subtracts 1320 − 1250 as ordinary numbers, but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

questions.title: Ch 19 Logo · Triangle track
questions.prompt:
A toy car drives around a track shaped like an equilateral triangle.

Every inside angle is 60°.

The toy car moves forward 25 steps and turns right, 3 times.

In Logo this is `REPEAT 3 [FD 25 RT ?]`.

- `FD 25` means move forward 25 steps (a length).
- `RT ?` means turn right by ? degrees (an angle).

How many degrees is each turn?
questions.figure_alt: A equilateral triangle walked by a toy car that starts facing right: arrows 1 to 3 are forward 25 steps each; one inside angle of 60° is marked; at each corner a dashed straight-on line and a right turn marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
The toy car turns by how much its direction changes:

- Straight on is a turn of \(0^\circ\).
- Turning round to go back is \(180^\circ\).
- The equilateral triangle's inside angle is \(60^\circ\), so the turn is

\[180^\circ - 60^\circ = \boxed{120^\circ}\]

Check: 3 turns make one full spin, \(3\times120^\circ = 360^\circ\), so the toy car ends facing right again.

\(60^\circ\) is the inside angle, not the turn: the turn is measured from the dashed straight-on line.

questions.title: Ch 19 Logo · Pentagon room
questions.prompt:
A robot vacuum cleans around a room shaped like a regular pentagon (every inside angle is 108°).

The robot vacuum moves forward 15 steps and turns right at each corner, all the way round.

- `FD 15` means move forward 15 steps (a length).
- `RT` means turn right by that many degrees (an angle).

Which commands draw it?
questions.figure_alt: A regular pentagon walked by a robot vacuum that starts facing down to the right: arrows 1 to 5 are forward 15 steps each; one inside angle of 108° is marked; at each corner a dashed straight-on line and a right turn marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Count the sides and look at one corner:

- The shape has 5 sides, so the commands repeat \(5\) times.
- Straight on (the dashed line) is a turn of \(0^\circ\).
- Turning round to go back is \(180^\circ\).
- The inside angle is \(108^\circ\), so the turn is

\[180^\circ - 108^\circ = 72^\circ\]

Check: \(5\times72^\circ = 360^\circ\), one full spin, so the robot vacuum is back at the start, facing down to the right.

\[\boxed{\texttt{REPEAT 5 [FD 15 RT 72]}}\]

`REPEAT 5 [FD 15 RT 108]` uses the inside angle: the robot vacuum turns the wrong amount, \(5\times108^\circ = 540^\circ\), so it does not draw a regular pentagon. `REPEAT 4 [FD 15 RT 72]` repeats only 4 times: \(4\times72^\circ = 288^\circ\), less than a full spin, so the shape does not close. `REPEAT 5 [FD 15 RT 90]` uses the turn for a square: \(5\times90^\circ = 450^\circ\), not one full spin of \(360^\circ\).

takeaway:
- Draw it first: a picture shows which rule to use.
- Check that the answer makes sense in the picture.
